author: Wealthy Content
title: Advantages of the Individual Investor - Wealthy Content
text:
Advantages of the Individual Investor Posted on by Wealthy Content
One thing that I really enjoy about the whole personal finance and financial independence (FI) community is that so many things have been thought of. I sometimes think about something I am doing pretending that I am smart and when I go and read about it, it has been done multiple times. This is the same with being an individual investor.
Normally in this community the rule of thumb is to invest in low-cost index funds, keep them for a long-term and voila! This is great advice in my opinion and advice which I also follow. I have monthly debit orders going into purchasing locally listed ETFs. Our TFSAs are in ETFs and as far as possible our retirement funds mimic indexes. Even the portion of our wealth which I invest through international brokerage is 57% invested in index trackers.
So, I am a fan and I would suggest buying low-cost index trackers to most people who want to invest for the long-term with a more hands-off approach. To find out almost anything on this you can head over to Bogleheads or for more South African content check out JustOneLap . As regular readers may know I unfortunately have a fascination with the market and more specifically buying and holding quality stocks like The Motley Fool’s mantra. The reason is that I believe individual investors have certain advantages compared to the big shot fund damagers managers.
I know this is not for everyone and that is why I would never recommend this to friends and family who are not genuinely attracted to buying individual stocks. So, as I were reading about all the advantages of the individual investor low and behold ChooseFI did a podcast last month on the exact same subject with Brian Feroldi who is writing for the Motley Fool. As I said, I always think I am smart only to realise I am late to the party. I would recommend listening to the podcast if you are interested in this subject as it is very educational. Brian’s strategy is also far more intense than mine with him having positions in around 80 individual stocks. It is similar in the fact that it does not use complex derivatives but only buys shares outright. There are some duplicates, but here is my list of advantages that I have personally found as individual investor who only has an internet connection, PC and brokerage account. Timeframe
This was the first point on the podcast as well, but it is something I would like to elaborate on. Being an individual investor, you can set your own timeframe. Not only should you not be worrying about quarterly results and short-term price moves. But you can decide what money to invest. You can look at a company and decide to purchase the stock with the intention of never selling it. This is probably one of the greatest reasons why Warren Buffet has been so successful with holding stocks like Coca Cola for more than 25 years.
The easy way for someone pursuing FI to do this is to invest money they do not need in the short term. This comes from the building blocks of paying off debt and having an emergency fund. Once you have these in place any money you invest in stocks is probably not needed in the medium- to long-term. Meaning there are no pressure like debt funding, margin calls etc, just good old buying a stock. Fund Managers normally do not have this luxury due to various reasons. Clients also expect fast and consistent results. This allows you to take a long-term/top-down/macro perspective on a stock like venture capitalists normally would . Stop Losses
Stop losses is a control used to minimise potential losses and crucial when trading derivatives . These are also used by fund managers when prices of stocks they bought fall too far. Funds have rules that govern them, and these are common to protect the value of the overall fund. This can even happen even when the manager believes his principles for buying the stock originally is still sound.
I will take a personal example. I bought General Electric (GE) shares earlier this year. My basic principle was that if the company was broken up it was worth more than its market cap at that point in time. As a safety net its dividend yield was higher than 3% at purchase although dividends were cut in November 2017 for only the second time since the great depression and might be cut again. These shares were down by more than 25% at some stage and as of this writing probably around the -20% mark. Funds might have been forced to sell this share by now. I have no such obligation and my base principles have been confirmed even more by the price drop. This could turn out bad (really bad), but I still believe GE has a lot of potential 5 – 10 years from now. The point is I have the choice, which is not always the case for the manager. Rebalancing
Another rule which a fund might have. If a fund manager buys a stock which grows by a massive amount it will become a large percentage of the fund’s overall value. In this case the manager might be forced to sell some of the stock and use the proceeds to buy something else. This is to avoid the concentration risk of having too much invested in one asset/stock.
As an individual investor you have no such rules. Why would you sell a good thing? You can rather not invest in it further or decide how much risk you are willing to take further. If it has brought you this much it needs to fall a lot before it is less than the index return. I have a couple of these in my portfolio, the one I have been invested in the longest is Apple (AAPL) which now is 17% of my portfolio. My rule is to not have more than 50% individual shares in my brokerage portfolio. Therefore, my last purchase was in an index ETF as the ratio was becoming quite close. In the meantime, there is no reason for me to sell AAPL, the company seems to still have a lot going for it. Smaller Stocks
Another advantage mentioned in the podcast. As an individual investor you can buy companies that does not meet fund requirements or are not included in available indexes. My smallest purchase is in a company called Sea Ltd (SE). This is a very risky investment and the share price is hugely volatile. At face value a loss-making company with negative cashflow hardly seems like a good investment. In the long-term, I believe SE actually has a lot going for it. This is a stock that can totally erase my investment or become a 10X (or more) machine. The advantage is that the choice in allocation is mine and as an individual investor I at least have the option. Who does not want a small dark horse wager in their portfolio? I can buy-and-hold
This ties in with the timeframe but is my investment philosophy. I can buy-and-hold my investments for as long as I want. Funds are required to show consistent results over short periods. This means there will be consistent trading liquidity during these periods. I have not made a trade in the last 3 months. This I believe is a big advantage to the individual investor. Fees
Now this is controversial but there are no fees for owning stocks. Don’t get me wrong brokerage accounts itself can have fees but you would have paid them if you bought an ETF as well. With a large amount and the right brokerage account (something I am trying to fix) you will have no persistent fees by holding stocks. This might be splitting hairs as the S&P 500 ETF I hold only has a TER of 5 basis points. But it is true and some index ETFs can have a TER in excess of 0.5%. Conclusion
The goal of this post is really for people to realise there might be a third option out there. It is not just index or fund to get stock market exposure. It can also give some perspective on why such a small percentage of fund managers actually beat the index . It is only for people who are really interested in buying individual stocks and even then, I would still suggest investing the majority of your stock market exposed investments in index tracking ETFs. In hindsight it has also been easy for me as it has been such a long bull market. I have had large exposure to tech stocks which has been in favour over this period. So, there has been a lot of luck as well. If the circumstances were different I might have written a different post. But you can make a bit of your own luck and if you are ever considering this, my opinion would be to start very small and do a ton of research in what you are buying.
Please remember none of this can be taken as financial advice and is purely my personal opinion.
Always grow your wealth for tomorrow while being content with your wealth today. Share this...
